Messages.Author: oaflord
Messages.Body:
Lately, I have seen a trend here in the Toronto area, in particular my
playgroup, that leans towards slim-lining the deck from 90 closer to 60
cards. Is there anyone out there that is noticing the same kind of trend
and if so, any suggestions as to why this is occuring now as opposed to
before (ie. release of Final Nights)?

I remember when Magic: The Gathering was relatively new, and deck size was
irrelevant, you just needed power. Then there was the introduction of speed
to the game, and all of a sudden you had to have JUST 60 cards in your deck,
otherwise you were not going to win. Now I know that MTG has card limits
and is an ENTIRELY different game, but are we (locally and globally) seeing
a trend towards slimming the deck down to get what you truly want and when
you want it?

On a side note that we may want to consider in another thread, but closely
parallels the slimming thing... Has VTES become somewhat degenerate in
deckbuilding? Some decks that I have seen over the last 4-6 months that
include only 5-10 different cards and NUMEROUS copies of those cards...
these decks seem to be winning! A good example was the !TOR deck I saw at
the Canadian Championship with multiple Embraces (20 I think), Art Scam,
Palla Grande and Presence Masters. This deck steam rolled it's way through
opponents. The "Spiradonas/Arika/anyone who can effectively use a Soul Gem"
decks also come to mind. Also, I am seeing more and more of the dreaded
Minion Tap/5th combo to the point that no one can do anything productive and
5 players get 1/2 a VP for their time. Now I have been known to use the
MT/5th, but I put the blood to good use and I just don't sit on it, waiting
for time to expire.

Basically I am concerned for the game. I see trends that bother me. I
agree people just want to win, but at what cost?

oAFLORD
aka
Thomas Kuster
VEKN Prince of Caledon

"oaflord" <oaf...@sprint.ca> schrieb im Newsbeitrag

> Lately, I have seen a trend here in the Toronto area, in particular my

> cards. Is there anyone out there that is noticing the same kind of trend
> and if so, any suggestions as to why this is occuring now as opposed to

Well, if you take a look at the decks packing significally fewer than 90
cards you will notice a trend: Each of these decks is not particularly fast
at burning through the library. And if this is the case, slimming the deck
greatly enhances your chances of drawing the right card at the right time.

On the other hand I have yet to see a dedicated combat deck with less thatn,
say, 80 cards and not having troubles with depleting the library too fast.

> I remember when Magic: The Gathering was relatively new, and deck size was
> irrelevant, you just needed power. Then there was the introduction of
speed
> to the game, and all of a sudden you had to have JUST 60 cards in your
deck,
> otherwise you were not going to win. Now I know that MTG has card limits
> and is an ENTIRELY different game, but are we (locally and globally)
seeing
> a trend towards slimming the deck down to get what you truly want and when
> you want it?

You're on the right track with your assumption. Since M:TG has a card limit
of four, it becomes even more important to keep the deck size as close to
the minimum as possible which is even more cruical here, since you don't
replace cards at such a frantic pace as in V:TES.

> On a side note that we may want to consider in another thread, but closely
> parallels the slimming thing... Has VTES become somewhat degenerate in
> deckbuilding? Some decks that I have seen over the last 4-6 months that
> include only 5-10 different cards and NUMEROUS copies of those cards...
> these decks seem to be winning! A good example was the !TOR deck I saw at
> the Canadian Championship with multiple Embraces (20 I think), Art Scam,
> Palla Grande and Presence Masters. This deck steam rolled it's way
through
> opponents. The "Spiradonas/Arika/anyone who can effectively use a Soul
Gem"
> decks also come to mind. Also, I am seeing more and more of the dreaded
> Minion Tap/5th combo to the point that no one can do anything productive
and
> 5 players get 1/2 a VP for their time. Now I have been known to use the
> MT/5th, but I put the blood to good use and I just don't sit on it,
waiting
> for time to expire.
>
> Basically I am concerned for the game. I see trends that bother me. I
> agree people just want to win, but at what cost?

I think when constructing a deck for tournament play you basically want a
deck which performs at a certain consistency level. A tournament deck needs
a certain focus and with selecting fewer different cards you greatly
increase this consistency level by reducing the amount of randomness. In
other words: the fewer cards (and different cards) you choose for your deck,
the more consistent it performes no matter what your starting crypt and
opening hand is.

I can follow your arguments which lead to your concerns, but I can't quite
share them. If an abundance of diversity in a deck is replaced by focus then
it won't do any harm to the game itself.

Since you brought up a comparison to Magic I'm gonna pick it up ;-)... If a
Magic player selects a mono-red deck for a tournament he is supposed to kill
is enemy within a few turns... but such a dedicated burn deck is easily
disrupted as well - and sometimes by a single card.

Fortunately, game designers provided a fist full of cards against every deck
type out there for V:TES as well, so if a deck type starts to get overly
dominant, players and opposing decks will adapt.

I would start getting concerned if a single deck starts to win a row of
consecutive tournaments *regardless* of any other decks there. And even in
this case I'm sure that game designers at White Wolf would come up with new
stuff for the bold defenders in the next expansion.

Anyone with Embraces for trade? ;-)

Vampirically yours,

Sascha
Prince of Wels

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Oaflord wrote:
>>Lately, I have seen a trend here in the Toronto area, in particular my
playgroup, that leans towards slim-lining the deck from 90 closer to 60
cards. Is there anyone out there that is noticing the same kind of trend
and if so, any suggestions as to why this is occuring now as opposed to
before (ie. release of Final Nights)?>>

There was a lengthy discussion on this very topic (why you would play a deck
smaller than 90 cards) just a couple weeks ago. Personally, if I were going to
build a 60 card deck in VTES, I'd just take the exact same deck and multiply
all the individual cards by 1.5 to make a 90 card deck, but assuming you don't
have access to all the cards you need, or you need a particular card combo to
come off, a smaller deck is going to be more consistient.

>>Now I know that MTG has card limits and is an ENTIRELY different game, but
are we (locally and globally) seeing a trend towards slimming the deck down to
get what you truly want and when you want it?>>

Probably not. Sure, if you only have X of a given card and want to be sure to
draw it, having X of that card in a 60 card deck results in a more likely draw
occurance than having X in a 90 card deck, but in most cases, I'd simply prefer
to have 1.5X of all the given cards in a 90 card deck. Where issues arise is
when thereis a card you only have (or want) one of. If you only have 1 of these
cards, in a 60 card deck, you are going to draw it more often than in a 90 card
deck. But then, if this card is so vital, why not just include 2 in a 90 card
deck instead of 1 in a 60? Regardless, there are reasons to play a smaller
deck, and reasons to play a larger deck. I don't think that there is an
international trend or anything.

>>On a side note that we may want to consider in another thread, but closely
parallels the slimming thing... Has VTES become somewhat degenerate in
deckbuilding? Some decks that I have seen over the last 4-6 months that
include only 5-10 different cards and NUMEROUS copies of those cards...
these decks seem to be winning!>>

That is because if you have a good strategy, you might as well do it as good as
you can. There are currently two different general VTES worldviews on deck
building--the "focused" deck view and the "toolboxy" deck view. I, for one,
vastly prefer the "focused" deck design--do one thing really good, and unless
you run into the thing that stops you dead, you are going to be effective--as
opposed to the "toolboxy" deck design, where you do a lot of different things
and are always ready for any opponent. Neither one is inherrently better than
the other (well, I don't actually believe that, but I'll appear egalitarian for
this discussion), and both can result in winning (or losing) decks.

The main problem with the hyper focused deck is that it has a weakness (and I'm
not talking about a specific anti-deck X kind of weakness. I'm talking about a
general strategy that just shuts you down. My hyper focused Rush deck is good,
sure, but if I run into Gangrel anything, I pretty much am dead from the get
go). They all do. And when they are faced with such a weakness, then just lose.
If, however, you enter a tournament with a super focused deck that has one
vital weakness, but no one happens to be playing any decks that capitalize upon
that weakenss, you are going to do really well. This isn't a problem with the
focused deck, however, it is just how the game works.

>>Also, I am seeing more and more of the dreaded Minion Tap/5th combo to the
point that no one can do anything productive and 5 players get 1/2 a VP for
their time.>>

Intercept their 5th actions, for instance. Or, rush their vampires so they lose
all their blood before they are minion tapped.

>>Basically I am concerned for the game. I see trends that bother me. I
agree people just want to win, but at what cost?>>

All of these decks have existed for years and years, and the game hasn't fallen
apart. Super focused decks are part of the game design. They are strong, but
easily unhinged, and if you unhinge them, they simply lose.

> No need to appear egalitarian for us, I am interested in people's opinions

Well, I know Peter is one of the True Believers in Focus, and I'm heavily
weighted towards focus myself, but there is definitely an advantage (always
prepared!) in playing a toolbox deck. That being said, I'd rather take my
chances with a focused deck.

I guess the main problem occurs when someone plays a focused, common deck.
Sure, they bleed really well, but how common is Deflection as a bleed
defense? It's much easier to focus in slightly off-kilter decks. Such as a
Rush deck. Fortitude, Obedience (ltos of it) or agg damage will really kill
a mono-pot (or nearly so) deck, but very little else will.

> I concur that focussed decks do have a weakness, as do the self-titled
> degenerate decks that I have mentioned, but if a deck has enough of a
focus,
> can a person really expect a toolbox deck or a general strategy to shut it

Yeah, it can be done. For example, take a potence rush deck (Peter's
industry-standard Nosferatu Hate You will do) vs. a Ventrue toolbox deck as
its prey. The rush deck can rush and hit stuff. The Ventrue toolbox deck
will be able to prevent some damage, deflect a few of the bleeds if
necessary, send some vote damage back to its predator, maybe have a little
intercept vs. hunts/rescues and probably use a couple of 5ths. None of
these alone is going to shut the rush deck down, but in the right
combination (having enough fortitude/obedience to shut down rush isn't too
hard), it can definitely happen.

> down? Perhaps, there is only one, maybe two focussed anti-decks to the
> degenerate deck and I can hope that no one plays it?

I'm not sure what you're getting at here. In general, focused decks are not
KO'ed by a specific *other* deck. Rather, they are killed by running into a
specific strategy that the opposing deck (full of its strange other-ness)
employs, such as intercept, or fortitude for combat defense. Lots of
tournament decks don't include any combat defense (other than S:CE), and so
fall prey to IG rush. Substitute (me for him...your coke for gin) fortitude
for S:CE, and you haven't lost much against other non-combat decks (except
perhaps the Majesty untap), but against real combat decks, you've gained a
lot.

Xian

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija

Oaflord wrote:
>>No need to appear egalitarian for us, I am interested in people's opinions
in regards to toolbox vs. focus as well.
I thought this might be an offshoot of this query.>>

Yeah, ok, the cat is out. I don't really like toolbox decks. I have nothing
against them, and have seen good ones, but I generally prefer to use a deck
that is really good at one thing than a deck that is not so good at a lot of
stuff. But then most of my decks use only one discipline anyways, so that only
makes sense.

>>I concur that focussed decks do have a weakness, as do the self-titled
degenerate decks that I have mentioned, but if a deck has enough of a focus,
can a person really expect a toolbox deck or a general strategy to shut it
down?>>

Sure. Depends on what the focused deck does and how solid the toolbox deck is.
My Rush deck, for instance, which is hyper focused, is often foiled simply
because my prey has a few good combat defense cards (Obediance or Flesh of
Marble, say) at the right time. They don't even have to have a lot of them,
just have them at the right time. The toolbox deck's advantage is that it is
ready for anything, and if it can draw the right defenses at the right time, it
is going to do well.

>>Perhaps, there is only one, maybe two focussed anti-decks to the degenerate
deck and I can hope that no one plays it?>>

Nah--it isn't about that. This isn't a situation like that Necropotence deal in
Magic in, what, 1995 or something (when all the good decks were either
Necropotence decks or specifically anti-necropotence decks). It is about
general strategies being useful against hyper focused ones--they just need to
be the right strategies. Again, using my Rush deck as an example (my Rush deck
is as hyper focused as they come--it does nothing but kill. No untap. No
intercept. No vote defense. Limited pool management. Limited bleed bonus. Just
Rush/IG.), it is a good deck that can be very sucessful, but it is easily
foiled by:

-Manuver based defenses.
-Heavy fortitude.
-Heavy obediance.
-Anything Gangrel.
-Decks that hit back.
-Long ranged combat.
-Weenie horde decks.

That is seven different strategies right off the top of my head that make my
deck much less effective, if not completely shut down. Why my deck works is
because I am capitalizing upon the general lack of combat defense (other than
Majesty) that you see in tournament play. If people played more combat defense
(or offense), for instance, my deck would be much less effective. Super focused
decks are all about playing the odds.

Messages.Author: Ian Lee
Messages.Body:
>No need to appear egalitarian for us, I am interested in people's opinions
>in regards to toolbox vs. focus as well.
>I thought this might be an offshoot of this query.

Beyond whether a deck is toolbox or focused, there's also the environment it
will play in.

In general, I would expect a toolbox deck to do poorly in a heavily focused
environment. And, I would expect a focused deck to do poorly in a heavily
toolboxed environment. To an extent, it's because of the balance between
threats and answers, but putting that aside, I'd still expect these based on
psychology. An environment weighted one way or the other is likely to
appreciate decks of its ilk. In other words, you want to avoid playing a deck
that people hate because they may consciously or unconsciously try to screw it.

>I concur that focussed decks do have a weakness, as do the self-titled
>degenerate decks that I have mentioned, but if a deck has enough of a focus,
>can a person really expect a toolbox deck or a general strategy to shut it
>down? Perhaps, there is only one, maybe two focussed anti-decks to the
>degenerate deck and I can hope that no one plays it?

Results will tend to indicate whether there's a problem with a particular deck
type, though heavily metagaming against a particular deck will reduce its VPs
without reducing its metagame impact.

In message <3b968ce8$0$594$ba62...@nntp02.dk.telia.net>, Jesper Bøje
<26984...@mail1.stofanet.dk> writes

>Just wated to hear if my play group is the only one playing with tower
>decks, we have a 4CL and still I have a deck with between 400 and 500 cards.

In general, a deck this size would be uncompetitive in a standard
environment because you can't ever have any certainty of what you're
going to draw. You can't make combat attacks knowing you'll be able to
back them up. You can't make a bleed knowing you'll be able to back it
up with stealth. etc.

The standard is also no limits, which significantly changes the
environment again.

>Basically alot of decks there is played is a clan, all the vampiers of that
>clan, all the cards fitting into that clan, based on the clan and their
>disiplins, and we are having alot of fun with it.

That's cool - it's just a very, very different environment.

>I NEVER understood why
>there is a card MAX in the Rules, well not a rule we are using I guess

Because the game doesn't have a card limit otherwise.

With a card limit, the trade-offs come between putting more cards in and
maximising the probability of getting the cards you want.

Frex:
You have 60 cards in your deck. 6 of them (let's say a 6CL) are
Deflections. The overall proportion is 10%. If you then move the deck
up to 120 cards, the proportion is 5% - much less likely to draw one.

With a deck limit, but no individual card limit, the decisions come
based instead on what you include. You can include some of everything
or a lot of one thing, or somewhere in between. So you can make a deck
with a huge capacity for *something* - whatever that might be is your
choice.

Think of it as the difference between going on holiday with one suitcase
only, which you can put whatever you want in. On the other hand, you
can take as many suitcases as you want but only X swim-suits or X t-
shirts etc.

Messages.Author: Chris Berger
Messages.Body:
> No need to appear egalitarian for us, I am interested in people's opinions
> in regards to toolbox vs. focus as well.
> I thought this might be an offshoot of this query.
>

Since I haven't posted in a bit, I'll get into this one. I believe in
a certain degree of focus. If you're gonna build a bleed deck, don't
include votes. If you're gonna build a vote deck, don't include rush.
That much, I guess, is obvious. However, it's tough to just do one
thing. Even the best bleed deck needs either combat, stealth, or some
way (such as tapping, seduction, or dawn op) to be unblockable. If
they do anything besides bruise and bleed, they'll also need combat
defense/avoidance.

Essentially, each deck needs to know how it will defend against each
other broad achetype of deck. The answer could be nothing, but you at
least have to address that. I break this down into 4 areas, 1 of
offense (how are you going to get your prey to 0 pool) and 3 of
defense. For example, a standard rush deck with have the following
plan of action:

Offense: rush (forcing him to influence more) and swarm bleed
Combat defense: fight back
Bleed defense: rush the bleeders
Vote defense: intimidation/rush

Note that this is all accomplished by the rush action and combat, so
you're all set. You can focus entirely on your primary objective. A
Lasombra bruise and bleed, on the other hand, might have the following
plan:

Offense: bleed (intimidation)
Combat defense: fight back
Bleed defense: wake and deflect (debatable... could be intercept or
rush)
Vote defense: titles/DOM (again debatable... you could add some rush
or DT)

A Malkavian S&B might go with:

Offense: bleed (stealth)
Combat defense: wake and obedience
Bleed defense: wake and deflect (could also be telepathic counter)
Vote defense: wake and Delaying Tactics

Note that this isn't necessarily all there is to a deck, but once
you've gotten these four areas taken care of, they should encompass
all but about 5 cards out of your deck (some people fill the whole
deck this way), with most of the cards being offensive in nature. The
last 3 to 5 cards, I use as "prayer cards". These are cards which you
won't often need, but which will come in handy against a certain deck.
Maybe an Illegal Search and Seizure or a Deal with the Devil, or a
Malkavian Dementia (these are all masters, but minion cards work as
prayer cards too). The idea is, when you get into one of those
situations where you're pretty much screwed, you often get real pissed
off if there's nothing in the deck to hope for. If you've got the
right card in there somewhere, then you sit and pray for it, hoping
that it just might be the next card. If you have enough card cycling,
then you throw away everything looking for it and it just might save
you. But don't overdo it, or you'll be pitching away Canine Hordes
and Letters From Vienna all game.

Messages.Body:
pete...@icqmail.com (PeterM) wrote in message news:<5802b3d0.01090...@posting.google.com>...

> Because you maintain a 7 hand size in VTES, and running out of your
> library is bad, the ONLY reason i can see to making a 60-card deck is
> if you want X card to come up Y times, but you have very few of X, so
> you reduce the deck size to increase the chance. And you can't even do
> it for a combat deck.
>

There *is* one other good reason for playing a smaller deck, assuming
that you are pretty sure you're not going to run out of cards (i.e.
it's a slow deck). If you have a 90 card deck with 9 Golcondas in
it, you can expect a Golconda every 10 cards. That's the expectation.
I'm a bit rusty on my statistics, but the standard deviation is the
amount by which you might expect to deviate from that 10 card
interval. Something like 90% of the time, you will not go more than
(10 + 2 standard deviations) cards without getting a Golconda. If you
make the deck smaller, say a 60 card deck with 6 Golcondas in it, the
expectation is still 10 cards per Golconda that you pull, however the
standard deviation is smaller.

If I remembered more statistics, I'd calculate it for you. Maybe
someone else wants to? But the point is that the deck will be more
consistent. Both decks will, on average, give you a Golconda every 10
cards, but with the 90 card deck you're more likely to go 15 cards,
get one, then go 5 cards and get a second.

That said, the vast majority of decks still benefit from playing with
the full 90 cards. Only if the deck is extremely slow and doesn't
expect to get through the deck even while sitting at a table full of
bloat decks should it consider cutting back on quantity in favor of
consistency.

Last tournament I played in, I played a 75 card stealth bleed deck. Never came
close to running out of cards in 3 rounds.

Only recently, say, in the last year, have I made attempts to build serious
tournament decks. The best decks I've put together in that time have all been
less than 90. In part, I believe it has to do with the mentality I'm using
when putting the deck together. If the deck can't be larger than, say, 80, I
know I can't add fluff or prayer cards. Every card is judged harshly. OTOH,
if I allow myself to go up to 90, I let more iffy cards slide. I allow more
themes to creep in.

There is one group of decks I don't think I can make smaller decks for - vote
decks. Too many times I'll be happy with my tight 80 card vote deck and, then,
discover I hadn't put any vote cards in yet.

And, I doubt I'd go under 90 with a celerity based deck unless I didn't care
whether I ran out of cards. But, the vast majority of my tournament decks are
going to be under 90, at least as long I approach tournaments as I do now.

Messages.Author: James Coupe

In message <9o0f84$87j$1...@scavenger.euro.net>, Khris
<griev...@hotmail.com> writes

>Well, I didn't make up the house rules. I asked why there was a 6CL limit,
>and was told that it was to prevent abuse of certain cards...

Your players do not understand the game if they believe 6CL prevents
"abuse".

For example:

Under 6CL, all defences for stealth and bleed are reduced in nature.
However, Stealth and Bleed has sufficient repeat cards that it can still
present an extremely focused deck.

Under 6CL, all defences against Strike: Combat Ends are significantly
reduced. 18 copies of Presence based Strike: Combat Ends are available.
A Tremere deck has fewer ways to advance in combat. A Brujah deck has
fewer ways to advance in combat, and so on.

In general, the basic functionality cards are repeated a number of
times. The cards designed to facilitate advance around them are not
(limited to one or two for any given discipline, say, and not repeated
across them all).

The game was designed with this in mind. There are more available forms
of advance than defence, in general (for instance, there are many ways
to deal damage in combat, damage limitation is reserved for a few
disciplines). A Gangrel deck is *supposed* to be able to go for lots of
stealth if the player wants it. A weenie deck is supposed to be able to
Computer Hack like there's no tomorrow. That's how the game was
designed.

If what you players actually mean when they say abuse is
"repetitiveness", this is entirely separate.

There are many, many threads regarding this in the newsgroup, archived
at www.google.com

>along the lines of Country. What would that need to work, and what sort of
>deck do you think is best?

Well, combat always seems a sensible option to pursue.

Path of the Feral Heart, Mythic Form, Flesh of Marble, Sideslip, Taste
of Vitae and Blur seems a good place to start, with some minor stealth
knocking around (Swallowed by the Night gives you a potential maneuver),
possibly a Disguised Weapon/Gun combo, if all else fails, and Claws of
the Dead/Bone Spur[0]. (The gun is also useful if you find yourself up
against S:CE, where you don't have to "waste" combat cards if you don't
want to, except to cycle.) Psyche! is also going to be useful, for S:CE
"defence".

I'd also be tempted to drop in two or three Sacrificial Lamb for blood
gain, possibly a couple of Gangrel Conspiracy in case. A few Night
Moves for edge stealing and minor bleeds. A Laptop or two, or a
Computer Hacking or two will give you some invaluable bleed punch, given
you can't guarantee combat so easily. One or two Hidden Lurkers (enough
for surprise, insufficient for guarantee) may prove useful in the
instance of a cocky Presence combat ends deck. I'd add Changeling Skin
Mask - bolsters the weenies or provides some intercept.

Of course, my natural instincts are to toolbox[1] slightly. (As a
result, I'd add a copy of City Gangrel Connections, probably.) Which
probably makes Storage Annex quite useful. All the "usual candidates"
are up for grabs - Wake, Blood Doll, Arson and so forth - depending on
your play-group. A sport bike and/or an intercept location (KRCG, Rumor
Mill, London Evenings Star) is probably useful, too.

How you choose to get into combat is up to you, of course. Bum's Rush
and/or Haven Uncovered is usually preferred, of course.

[0] I have always preferred Claws of the Dead to Wolf Claws because of
the maneuver option, rather than the press. If you do your job
properly, they don't get to presses. :) However, I have seen Bone Spur
used well, to facilitate defence against "Dodge" or minor damage
prevention (e.g. Leather Jacket, inferior Fortitude) - which given I've
suggested Blur seems sensible.

[1] A deck where the focus of your deck is slightly watered down to
provide other options. Often considered the opposite of "focus" which
does one narrow channel of things *well*, hoping that the speed and
efficiency bonus will help, trying to use the flexibility inherent in
its actions to scupper other decks (e.g. a rush deck performing a cross-
table rush, if it has to; a political deck banishing a vampire cross-
table, if it has to) rather than providing specific defence for those
actions.

And one day, I'll stick my reading head on and learn the difference
between City and Country.

In terms of Country/Normal , I'd be tempted to add:

Haaken Mortensen - he's perfect, because he has the "move a blood to a
Gangrel or Gangrel antitribu in your uncontrolled region" thing,
along with an ANI/FOR/PRO set of disciplines.
Omaya is also excellent - the built in damage prevention is cool, even
if you have AUS pro, rather than the (perhaps) more useful PRO
aus.

Leon and Sadie are obvious candidates if you want to weenify the deck,
pick the disciplines as you see fit, obviously.

Genevieve is a large, but useful, option to consider. Has 1 vote and
also has the potential to cast the three from the Priscus vote (or stall
it, maybe).

A deck with two or three Haaken, a copy of Omaya, a copy of Raven, a
copy of Camille Devereux and a copy of Gitanne St. Clair (ANI FOR PRO
Primogen) has the potential for an absolutely fantastic solid base.
Lots of solid mid-range discipline power.

Weeniefy as appropriate.

You can use the !Gangrel to diablerise with Gangrel Conspiracy, as
appropriate. Scorpion Sting provides your added damage, with Mythic
Form helping, but being quite expensive. Path of the Feral Heart is
much, much less useful here, unfortunately - Gangrel Antitribu only.
Adding Eco-Terrorists may well work out well, depending on the rest of
your crypt. I also like having vote power, so I'd be tempted to add one
copy of City Gangrel Connections. (For your Country Gangrel deck, too.)

You have the potential for a lot of untap (Freak Drive, Cat's Guidance)
and some unblockability when you need it (Dawn Operation, Daring the
Dawn, ignore Horrific Countenance :) ). Bleed power can come through
well targeted Force of Will.

You also have quite a bit of intercept available - Raptor, Raven Spy,
Cat's Guidance. Use some for defence - you lack bleed bounce - or rush
your predator as necessary to take out his bleeders, if that becomes an
issue.
